questions.q: Which statement best describes congruent figures?
questions.a: Same shape and size, so one fits exactly over the other
o: Same shape and size, so one fits exactly over the other
Same shape, but their sizes may be quite different from each other
Same size, but their shapes may be different from each other
Same shape and size, but only when neither one has been flipped

questions.q: Two rectangular notice boards are to be made congruent. Which measurements must be the same?
questions.a: Length and breadth of each
o: Length and breadth of each
Only the length of each board
Only the breadth of each board
Its length and the angle at one corner

questions.q: Which of these is NOT allowed while checking two figures for congruence by superimposing?
questions.a: Stretching one figure to fit the other
o: Stretching one figure to fit the other
Rotating one figure before placing it down
Flipping one figure over before placing it
Turning one figure through a half turn first

questions.q: A fitter checks two steel brackets. Each has arms of 10 cm and 6 cm, but the angle between the arms is 60° on one and 75° on the other. What can he conclude?
questions.a: Not congruent, as the angle also fixes the bracket
o: Not congruent, as the angle also fixes the bracket
Congruent, because both arm lengths match on the two brackets
Congruent, because one can be rotated onto the other bracket
Not congruent, because the two arms must be equal to each other

questions.q: Hasina cuts a paper arrow from one notice. She turns the arrow over and it covers the arrow on another notice exactly. What does this show?
questions.a: The two arrows are congruent, since flipping is allowed
o: The two arrows are congruent, since flipping is allowed
The arrows are not congruent, since flipping changes the figure
The arrows are congruent only if they are the same way up
Nothing, until the arrow is also stretched a little

questions.q: Sunita says: 'Two rectangles are congruent whenever their longer sides are both 10 cm.' Do you agree? Support your answer with measurements.
questions.a: No. Take 10 cm by 4 cm and 10 cm by 6 cm. Both have a longer side of 10 cm but the breadths differ, so they do not fit over each other. Both length and breadth must match.
s: Verdict: Sunita is wrong
Counterexample such as 10 by 4 and 10 by 6
States that length and breadth must both be equal

questions.q:

Reason (R): A rectangle is fixed by its length and its breadth.
questions.a: A is false but R is true.
o: A is false but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.

questions.q:
Match what must be measured to copy each figure (Column I) with the measurements (Column II).
Column I: 1. A circle  2. A rectangle  3. A steel bracket with two arms meeting at a corner  4. A square
Column II: a. Length of one side  b. The radius  c. Length and breadth  d. Both arm lengths and the angle ABC
(a) Circle P has radius 7 cm. What radius must a circle have to be congruent to P? (b) Rani says a circle Q of diameter 15 cm is congruent to P. Is she right? Give the reason.
questions.a: (a) 7 cm. (b) No. Q has radius 15 / 2 = 7.5 cm, which is not 7 cm, so Q is larger and cannot fit exactly over P.
s: Part (a): radius 7 cm
Part (b): halves the diameter to 7.5 cm and says not congruent

questions.q: (a) Is a rectangle 9 cm by 4 cm congruent to one that is 4 cm by 9 cm? What must be done to the second before superimposing? (b) Is it congruent to a rectangle 9 cm by 5 cm? Why?
questions.a: (a) Yes; rotate it (a quarter turn) so the 9 cm sides lie together. (b) No; the breadths 4 cm and 5 cm differ, so it cannot fit exactly.
s: Part (a): yes, after rotating so the 9 cm sides match
Part (b): no, because the breadths differ

questions.q: State what congruent figures are, and name the two movements that may be used while superimposing them.
questions.a: Congruent figures have the same shape and size and can be fitted exactly one over the other. The figure may be rotated or flipped.
s: Defines congruent figures as same shape and size
Names rotating and flipping

questions.q: The arms of the signboard symbol are AB = 4 cm and BC = 8 cm. (a) Why can these two lengths alone not recreate it exactly? (b) Which third measurement fixes it?
questions.a: (a) Many different symbols can be drawn with the same arm lengths, as the angle between the arms can change. (b) The angle ABC, for example 80°.
s: Part (a): says the angle between the arms can vary, giving different symbols
Part (b): names angle ABC

questions.q: A tailor cuts one patch from a paper pattern lying face up and another from the same pattern turned over. Are the two patches congruent? Give a reason.
questions.a: Yes. They have the same shape and size; one can be flipped over to fit exactly on the other.
s: Says yes, congruent
Gives the reason that flipping is allowed so they fit exactly

questions.q:
Read the statements about congruent figures.
Statement 1: Two circles are congruent whenever their radii differ by less than 1 cm.
Statement 2: A rectangle 7 cm by 3 cm is congruent to a rectangle 3 cm by 7 cm.
Statement 3: Two symbols with the same two arm lengths can still be non-congruent.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: 2 and 3 only
o: 2 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q: Write the measurements of three rectangles R1, R2, R3 such that R1 and R2 are congruent although R2 is turned, and R3 has the same longer side as R1 but is not congruent to it.
questions.a: Example: R1 is 12 cm by 5 cm. R2 is 5 cm by 12 cm (turned through a quarter turn, so congruent). R3 is 12 cm by 7 cm: same longer side, different breadth, not congruent.
s: R1 and R2 with the same two sides in swapped order
R3 with the same longer side
Says R3 differs in breadth so it is not congruent

questions.q: A signmaker's arrow-head has arms of 5 cm and 9 cm with 70° between them. Copy X has arms 5 cm and 9 cm with 70° between. Copy Y has arms 9 cm and 5 cm with 70° between, drawn the other way round. Copy Z has arms 5 cm and 9 cm with 110° between. Which copies are congruent to the arrow-head? Give reasons.
questions.a: X and Y are congruent: the same two arms and the same angle between them (Y is the arrow-head turned or flipped). Z is not, because its angle between the arms is 110°, not 70°.
s: X is congruent: same arms and angle
Y is congruent: turning or flipping is allowed
Z is not: the angle differs

questions.q: Honey runs a sign shop in a Jaipur market. (a) What one measurement fixes a circular sign? (b) What measurements fix a rectangular sign? (c) A customer wants a copy of a symbol with two arms meeting at a corner. Which three measurements must Honey copy? (d) The customer gives only the arms, 5 cm and 9 cm. Explain why Honey cannot promise a congruent copy.
questions.a: (a) The radius. (b) Length and breadth. (c) Both arm lengths and the angle between them. (d) With arms 5 cm and 9 cm the angle can take many values, giving different non-congruent symbols, so the angle must be given too.
s: Part (a): the radius
Part (b): length and breadth
Part (c): both arms and the included angle
Part (d): explains the angle can vary so copies differ

questions.q: A school wants to check two big rectangular boards (2.4 m by 1.2 m and 1.2 m by 2.4 m) and two small leaf-shaped cutouts for congruence. (a) For which pair would you measure, and for which would you trace and superimpose? (b) Check the boards by measuring. (c) What movement is used to place one board over the other? (d) Why can two lengths not settle the leaf cutouts?
questions.a: (a) Measure the boards (too big to trace); trace/superimpose the leaf cutouts. (b) Both are 2.4 m by 1.2 m, so congruent. (c) A quarter turn. (d) A leaf outline has no short list of lengths that fixes it, so it must be placed over the other.
s: Part (a): measuring for boards, superimposing for leaves
Part (b): both 2.4 m by 1.2 m, congruent
Part (c): rotation
Part (d): irregular shape needs superimposing

questions.q:
The Gram Panchayat wants steel brackets congruent to a template: arms of 10 cm and 6 cm with 60° between them. The gate needs 50 such brackets at ₹40 each. The storeroom shelves need 25 brackets of any shape. Lot A has 30 brackets with arms 10 cm and 6 cm and 60° between. Lot B has 20 with arms 6 cm and 10 cm and 60° between. Lot C has 25 with arms 10 cm and 6 cm and 75° between, offered at ₹20 each.
(a) Which lots are congruent to the template? (b) What is paid for the gate brackets? (c) An inspector checks only the arm lengths and passes all three lots at ₹40 each. How much extra is paid for lot C? (d) Should the Panchayat buy lot C for the shelves, or buy 25 more congruent brackets at ₹40 for them? Decide.
questions.a: (a) Lots A and B (lot B has the same arms and the same angle between them, turned over). Lot C has 75°. (b) 50 x 40 = ₹2,000. (c) 25 x 40 = ₹1,000, for brackets that cannot match the gate. (d) Buy lot C for the shelves: the shelves need no matching, so 25 x 20 = ₹500 against ₹1,000 saves ₹500; lot C must stay away from the gate.
s: Part (a): lots A and B, with the reason for B and why C fails
Part (c): ₹1,000 extra
Part (d): lot C for the shelves, saving ₹500, none at the gate

questions.q:
A tile shop in Surat shows four tiles. T1: circle of radius 10 cm. T2: circle of diameter 21 cm. T3: rectangle 30 cm by 20 cm. T4: rectangle 20 cm by 30 cm. Mrs Nair needs 40 tiles congruent to T1 at ₹45 each and 24 tiles congruent to T3 at ₹60 each from the shop. A wholesaler offers 24 tiles congruent to T3 at ₹54 each plus ₹200 for delivery.
(a) Which other tile, if any, is congruent to T1? (b) Which tile is congruent to T3? (c) What is the shop's price for her whole order? (d) For the 24 rectangular tiles, is the wholesaler cheaper? Decide.
questions.a: (a) None: T2 has radius 21 / 2 = 10.5 cm. (b) T4, a turned copy. (c) 40 x 45 + 24 x 60 = 1,800 + 1,440 = ₹3,240. (d) Wholesaler: 24 x 54 + 200 = ₹1,496 against ₹1,440 at the shop, so the shop is ₹56 cheaper; buy from the shop.
s: Part (a): none, because T2 has radius 10.5 cm
Part (b): T4
Part (d): ₹1,496 against ₹1,440, buy at the shop

questions.a: The patches are congruent by SSS

They are congruent only if cut the same way up

questions.q:
Read the statements about naming congruent triangles.
Statement 1: If ΔABC ≅ ΔXYZ, then ∠B = ∠Y.
Statement 2: If ΔABC ≅ ΔXYZ, it is also correct to write ΔACB ≅ ΔXYZ.
Statement 3: Circles of radii 5 cm and 9 cm drawn from the ends of a 7 cm segment meet at two points, and the two triangles formed are congruent.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 3 only

1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): If ΔABC ≅ ΔXYZ, then side BC equals side YZ.
Reason (R): In the name ΔABC ≅ ΔXYZ, the second vertex of the first triangle corresponds to the second vertex of the second.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.

questions.q:
ΔKAR ≅ ΔMUL. Match each part in Column I with its corresponding part in Column II.
Column I: 1. Vertex A  2. Side AR  3. Angle R  4. Side KR
Column II: a. Angle L  b. Side ML  c. Vertex U  d. Side UL
ΔHEN ≅ ΔBIG. (a) List the three pairs of corresponding sides. (b) In how many ways can this congruence be written in all, and why?
questions.a: (a) HE and BI, EN and IG, HN and BG. (b) 6 ways, since the three vertices of ΔHEN can be arranged in 6 orders and ΔBIG is written in the matching order.
s: Part (a): HE-BI, EN-IG, HN-BG
Part (b): 6 ways because 3 vertices can be ordered in 6 ways

questions.q: ΔABC and ΔDCB share the side BC, with AB = DC and AC = DB. (a) Name the condition that gives ΔABC ≅ ΔDCB and write the matching of vertices. (b) Which angle equals ∠ABC?
questions.a: (a) SSS: AB = DC, AC = DB and BC common (BC = CB). A goes with D, B with C, C with B. (b) ∠ABC = ∠DCB, as corresponding angles.
s: Part (a): SSS with the common side BC and the matching A-D, B-C, C-B
Part (b): ∠DCB

questions.q: In ΔLMN, LM = 6 cm, MN = 7.5 cm and LN = 9 cm. In ΔDEF, DE = 7.5 cm, EF = 9 cm and FD = 6 cm. Show the triangles are congruent and write the congruence in order.
questions.a: All three sides match (6, 7.5, 9), so SSS holds. L lies between sides 6 and 9, which meet at F; M between 6 and 7.5 at D; N between 7.5 and 9 at E. So ΔLMN ≅ ΔFDE.
s: Names SSS with the three equal side pairs
Writes ΔLMN ≅ ΔFDE by matching the vertices

questions.q: Ritu draws a 7 cm segment AB and circles of radii 5 cm and 9 cm from A and B. (a) Why do two triangles, ΔABE and ΔABF, appear? (b) Why does this not stop us using SSS?
questions.a: (a) The circles cross at two points, one on each side of AB. (b) The two triangles are mirror images in AB, so they are congruent; every triangle with these three sides is congruent.
s: Part (a): circles meet at two points on either side of AB
Part (b): the two triangles are congruent (AB is a line of symmetry)

questions.q: For ΔABC ≅ ΔXYZ, Aman writes ΔACB ≅ ΔXYZ. Why is this wrong, and how can the same congruence be written starting with ΔACB?
questions.a: The first, second and third vertices must correspond in order, but C corresponds to Z, not Y. The correct form is ΔACB ≅ ΔXZY.
s: Says the order of vertices does not match (C goes with Z)
Writes ΔACB ≅ ΔXZY

questions.q: Rectangle ABCD has AB = 9 cm and BC = 5 cm. Dev writes ΔABD ≅ ΔCBD, keeping B and D in place, because BD is common to both. Is his statement right? Give your reason.
questions.a: No. Writing ΔABD ≅ ΔCBD makes A match C and lays AB over CB. But AB = 9 cm and CB = 5 cm, so they do not overlap. The correct statement is ΔABD ≅ ΔCDB, with A matching C, B matching D and D matching B, so that AB = CD.
s: Verdict: Dev's statement is wrong
Shows AB (9 cm) would fall on CB (5 cm)
Gives the correct matching ΔABD ≅ ΔCDB

questions.q: In ΔABC, AB = 5 cm, BC = 6 cm and CA = 7 cm. In ΔXYZ, XY = 5 cm, YZ = 7 cm and ZX = 6 cm. Show that ΔABC ≅ ΔXYZ cannot be the correct way to write their congruence, and then write one that is correct.
questions.a: In ΔABC ≅ ΔXYZ, BC would match YZ, but BC = 6 cm and YZ = 7 cm. Matching equal sides instead: AB = YX = 5, BC = XZ = 6, CA = ZY = 7, so B goes with X, A with Y, C with Z. ΔABC ≅ ΔYXZ is correct.
s: Shows BC ≠ YZ so the order fails
Pairs the equal sides AB-YX, BC-XZ, CA-ZY
Writes ΔABC ≅ ΔYXZ

questions.q: Make up side lengths (all different numbers) for ΔABC and ΔPQR so that ΔABC ≅ ΔQRP. Write which sides are equal.
questions.a: Example: AB = 8 cm, BC = 10 cm, CA = 12 cm; QR = 8 cm, RP = 10 cm, PQ = 12 cm. In ΔABC ≅ ΔQRP, A goes with Q, B with R, C with P, so AB = QR, BC = RP, CA = PQ.
s: Gives three side lengths for each triangle that are equal in pairs
States AB = QR, BC = RP, CA = PQ
Checks the order A-Q, B-R, C-P

questions.q: In a kite ABCD, AB = AD = 6.5 cm and CB = CD = 9 cm. (a) Which two triangles are congruent, and by which condition? (b) Write the congruence in order. (c) List the three pairs of equal angles. (d) Does AC cut ∠BAD into two equal parts? Give a reason.
questions.a: (a) ΔABC and ΔADC, by SSS (AB = AD, CB = CD, AC common). (b) ΔABC ≅ ΔADC. (c) ∠BAC = ∠DAC, ∠BCA = ∠DCA, ∠B = ∠D. (d) Yes, since ∠BAC and ∠DAC are corresponding angles of congruent triangles.
s: Part (a): triangles and SSS with the common side
Part (b): ΔABC ≅ ΔADC
Part (c): three pairs of equal angles
Part (d): yes, corresponding angles are equal

questions.q: ΔHEN ≅ ΔBIG, with HE = 5.5 cm, EN = 6.5 cm and HN = 8 cm. (a) Write two other correct ways of stating the congruence. (b) Find BI, IG and BG. (c) Is ΔHEN ≅ ΔBGI correct? Check using the sides.
questions.a: (a) For example ΔEHN ≅ ΔIBG and ΔNEH ≅ ΔGIB. (b) BI = 5.5 cm, IG = 6.5 cm, BG = 8 cm. (c) No. It would make HE match BG, but HE = 5.5 cm and BG = 8 cm.
s: Part (a): two valid reorderings of both names
Part (b): BI = 5.5, IG = 6.5, BG = 8
Part (c): says no, and shows HE = 5.5 differs from BG = 8

questions.q:
Ms Sharma's school makes triangular flags for Independence Day. The template ΔPQR has PQ = 30 cm, QR = 40 cm and RP = 50 cm. Tailor A makes 50 flags with these sides. Tailor B makes 45 flags ΔLMN with LM = 40 cm, MN = 50 cm and NL = 30 cm. Tailor C makes 25 flags with sides 30 cm, 40 cm and 55 cm. The school pays ₹8 per flag congruent to the template and needs 120 flags.
(a) Which tailors' flags are congruent to the template? (b) Write ΔLMN's congruence with the template in order. (c) How much is paid, and how many flags are still short? (d) Should the school accept Tailor C's flags to finish at once, or ask for 25 new ones? Decide.
questions.a: (a) A and B (SSS); C has 55 cm, not 50. (b) L is between 40 and 30, which meet at Q; M between 40 and 50, at R; N between 50 and 30, at P. ΔPQR ≅ ΔNLM. (c) 95 x 8 = ₹760; 120 - 95 = 25 short. (d) Ask for 25 new ones: C's flags are not congruent, so the line would hang unevenly; accepting is defensible only if speed matters more than a uniform line.
s: Part (a): A and B by SSS, C rejected (55 cm)
Part (b): ΔPQR ≅ ΔNLM
Part (c): ₹760 and 25 short
Part (d): decision using the non-congruence of C

questions.q:
Sunil, a carpenter in Ludhiana, makes door panels as rectangles ABCD with AB = 90 cm and BC = 210 cm and cuts each along the diagonal BD to get two triangular panels. A contractor needs 36 identical triangular panels. Option 1: buy 18 rectangular sheets at ₹400 each and cut them. Option 2: buy 36 separate triangular sheets at ₹210 each.
(a) Write the lengths of CD and DA. (b) Which triangles are congruent, by what condition, and in what order? (c) Find the cost of each option. (d) Which option should the contractor choose? Justify using (b) and (c).
questions.a: (a) CD = 90 cm, DA = 210 cm. (b) ΔABD ≅ ΔCDB by SSS (AB = CD, AD = CB, BD common). (c) Cutting 18 rectangular sheets: 18 x 400 = ₹7,200. Buying 36 triangular sheets: 36 x 210 = ₹7,560. (d) Buying 18 rectangular sheets and cutting them is ₹360 cheaper, and every cut gives two congruent panels by SSS.
s: Part (a): CD = 90 cm, DA = 210 cm
Part (b): ΔABD ≅ ΔCDB by SSS
Part (d): chooses the cheaper rectangular-sheet plan with cost and congruence reasons

questions.q:
Match each set of equal parts in two triangles (Column I) with what it guarantees (Column II).
Column I: 1. Two sides and the angle between them  2. Two sides and an angle not between them  3. All three angles  4. All three sides
Column II: a. Congruence by SSS  b. Congruence by SAS  c. Same shape only, congruence not guaranteed  d. SSA, congruence not guaranteed
O is the midpoint of PS and also of QR. (a) Name the three equal parts of ΔPOQ and ΔSOR. (b) Write the congruence in order and say which side equals PQ.
questions.a: (a) PO = SO, QO = RO and ∠POQ = ∠SOR (vertically opposite angles). (b) ΔPOQ ≅ ΔSOR by SAS, so PQ = SR.

Part (b): ΔPOQ ≅ ΔSOR by SAS, PQ = SR

questions.q: Gauri says: 'Two triangles with equal sides of 8 cm and 6 cm and an equal angle of 35° are always congruent.' Is she right?
questions.a: Not always. If the 35° lies between the 8 cm and 6 cm sides, SAS makes them congruent. If it does not, it is the SSA case, where two different triangles may be possible, so she cannot be sure.
s: Verdict: not always
Congruent when the angle is included (SAS)
Not guaranteed when the angle is not included (SSA)

questions.q: State the SAS condition for congruence of triangles. What does 'included angle' mean?
questions.a: If two sides and the included angle of one triangle equal two sides and the included angle of the other, the triangles are congruent. The included angle is the angle between the two sides.
s: States SAS correctly
Explains included angle as the angle between the two sides

questions.q: ΔPQR has PQ = 8 cm, PR = 6.5 cm and ∠P = 62°. ΔLMN has LM = 8 cm, LN = 6.5 cm and ∠L = 62°. (a) Are they congruent? Name the condition and write the congruence. (b) QR is measured as 7.4 cm. What is MN, and why?
questions.a: (a) Yes, SAS (the 62° lies between the equal sides): ΔPQR ≅ ΔLMN. (b) MN = 7.4 cm, since QR and MN are corresponding sides.
s: Part (a): SAS and ΔPQR ≅ ΔLMN
Part (b): MN = 7.4 cm as corresponding sides

questions.q: Rafi draws PQ = 10 cm, a line from P at 35°, and an arc of radius 7 cm from Q to cut the line. (a) How many points can the arc cut the line at? (b) What does this say about SSA?
questions.a: (a) Two points, R and S, so two triangles fit the same measurements. (b) SSA (two sides and a non-included angle) does not guarantee congruence.
s: Part (a): the arc cuts the line at two points
Part (b): SSA does not guarantee congruence

questions.q: ΔABC has AB = 7 cm, BC = 6 cm, ∠B = 47°; ΔXYZ has XY = 7 cm, YZ = 6 cm, ∠Y = 47°. (a) Are they congruent? Name the condition. (b) If the 47° were ∠A and ∠X instead (same sides), could you still be sure?
questions.a: (a) Yes, SAS, ΔABC ≅ ΔXYZ, the angle being between the two sides. (b) No. The angle is then not included, which is the SSA case, and two different triangles can fit.
s: Part (a): congruent by SAS with the angle between the sides
Part (b): not sure, since it becomes SSA

questions.q: Show that equal angles alone cannot make two triangles congruent: describe two triangles with angles 50°, 60° and 70°.
questions.a: Draw one with a 5 cm side between the 50° and 60° angles, and another with a 10 cm side between the same angles. Both have angles 50°, 60°, 70°, but their sizes differ, so they are not congruent.
s: Both triangles have the same three angles
Gives different side lengths such as 5 cm and 10 cm
Concludes same shape but not congruent

questions.q: In ΔABC, AB = 7 cm, AC = 9 cm, ∠A = 65°. Write the three measurements for ΔXYZ that make ΔABC ≅ ΔXYZ by SAS, and name the matching vertices.
questions.a: XY = 7 cm, XZ = 9 cm, ∠X = 65°. A matches X, B matches Y, C matches Z.
s: Gives XY = 7 cm and XZ = 9 cm
Gives ∠X = 65° between them

questions.q: Priya cuts a metal triangle ΔPQR with PQ = 7 cm, PR = 5 cm and ∠QPR = 40°. Her helper cuts ΔXYZ with XY = 7 cm, XZ = 5 cm and ∠YXZ = 40°, but lays the metal face down, so ΔXYZ is a mirror image. (a) Which angle lies between the given sides in each triangle? (b) Is the helper's piece congruent? Name the condition. (c) Write the congruence in order. (d) QR is measured as 4.5 cm. Which side of ΔXYZ is 4.5 cm, and does flipping change this?
questions.a: (a) ∠QPR in ΔPQR and ∠YXZ in ΔXYZ. (b) Yes, SAS; flipping is allowed. (c) ΔPQR ≅ ΔXYZ. (d) YZ = 4.5 cm, since QR and YZ are corresponding sides; flipping a figure does not change its lengths.
s: Part (a): the included angles ∠QPR and ∠YXZ
Part (b): congruent by SAS, flipping allowed
Part (c): ΔPQR ≅ ΔXYZ
Part (d): YZ = 4.5 cm and flipping keeps lengths

questions.q: Compare two constructions. In (i) PQ = 9 cm, PR = 7 cm and ∠P = 40°. In (ii) PQ = 9 cm, QR = 7 cm and ∠P = 40°. (a) In which is the angle included? (b) Which condition applies to it? (c) For the other, why can two triangles be drawn? (d) Which one lets Rabia be sure of congruence?
questions.a: (a) (i): ∠P is between PQ and PR. (b) SAS. (c) In (ii) the 40° is not between the sides (SSA), and an arc of 7 cm from Q cuts the line from P at two points. (d) Construction (i), because SAS guarantees congruence.
s: Part (a): (i) has the included angle
Part (b): SAS
Part (c): arc cuts the line at two points in SSA
Part (d): (i) is certain

questions.q:
The fete committee cuts triangular rangoli sheets to match a template with two sides of 24 cm and 18 cm and 50° between them, and pays ₹5 for each sheet congruent to it. Four students cut sheets. Anil cuts 12 sheets with sides 24 cm and 18 cm and 50° between. Bela cuts 10 with 24 cm and 18 cm and 70° between. Chitra cuts 8 with sides 18 cm and 24 cm and 50° between. Dev cuts 6 with sides 24 cm and 20 cm and 50° between.
(a) Which students' sheets are congruent to the template? (b) For each of the others, say which part fails the SAS condition. (c) How much is paid? (d) The committee needs 30 matching sheets tonight. Anil can cut the 10 missing ones tomorrow at ₹5 each. Dev can supply 10 tonight at ₹3 each. Decide whom to ask.
questions.a: (a) Anil and Chitra, by SAS. (b) Bela's included angle is 70°, not 50°; Dev's second side is 20 cm, not 18 cm. (c) (12 + 8) x 5 = ₹100. (d) Wait for Anil. Dev's 10 sheets would save only 10 x (5 - 3) = ₹20 and, with a 20 cm side, would not match the other 20 sheets, which spoils the rangoli.
s: Part (a): Anil and Chitra
Part (b): Bela's angle and Dev's side fail
Part (c): ₹100
Part (d): asks Anil, citing the ₹20 saving against a mismatch

questions.q:
A gardener marks triangular flower beds with ropes. Bed 1 has sides 12 m and 9 m with 40° between them. Bed 2 has sides 9 m and 12 m with 40° between them. Bed 3 has sides 12 m and 9 m with 55° between them. Five beds are needed: three like bed 1 and two like bed 3. A stone-edging mould made for one shape can be reused for every congruent bed. The first mould costs ₹2,400 and a mould for bed 3 costs ₹5,000. The two beds like bed 3 could instead be re-marked with a 40° angle between the 12 m and 9 m sides for ₹800 each.
(a) Is bed 2 congruent to bed 1? Give the condition. (b) Is bed 3 congruent to bed 1? Give the reason. (c) What do the moulds cost if the five beds are made as planned? (d) Should the gardener re-mark the two beds? Decide.
questions.a: (a) Yes, SAS: the same two sides with the same angle between them. (b) No, the angle between the 12 m and 9 m sides is 55°, not 40°. (c) 2,400 + 5,000 = ₹7,400. (d) Re-marked, all five beds are congruent, so one mould is enough: 2,400 + 2 x 800 = ₹4,000, which saves ₹3,400; re-mark them.
s: Part (a): congruent by SAS
Part (b): not congruent, included angle differs
Part (d): ₹4,000 and a saving of ₹3,400, so re-mark

In ΔABC, ∠A = 48°, ∠C = 62° and BC = 6 cm. In ΔXYZ, ∠X = 48°, ∠Z = 62° and YZ = 6 cm. (a) Find ∠B and ∠Y. (b) Name the condition for ΔABC ≅ ΔXYZ and write it in order.
questions.a: (a) ∠B = 180° - 110° = 70° and ∠Y = 70°. (b) AAS (BC lies opposite ∠A, not between the given angles), or ASA once the third angles are found: ΔABC ≅ ΔXYZ.

Part (b): names AAS (or ASA after the third angle) and writes ΔABC ≅ ΔXYZ

Part (b): AB = AC and BD = DC

Part (b): AAS since QR is not between the angles

questions.q: Rina's triangle T1 has ∠B = 40°, BC = 7 cm and ∠C = 65°. Triangle T2 has ∠D = 75°, ∠E = 40° and EF = 7 cm. Triangle T3 has ∠K = 40°, ∠L = 65° and KM = 7 cm. (a) Find ∠A in T1. (b) Is T2 congruent to T1? Give the condition and write the congruence. (c) Is T3 congruent to T1? Explain using the position of the 7 cm side. (d) Change one measurement of T3 so that it becomes congruent to T1.
questions.a: (a) ∠A = 180° - 105° = 75°. (b) In T2, ∠F = 180° - 115° = 65°, so EF lies between 40° and 65° as BC does in T1: ASA (AAS as given), ΔABC ≅ ΔDEF. (c) No. In T3 the 7 cm side KM lies between ∠K = 40° and ∠M = 75°, not between 40° and 65°, so it does not correspond to BC. (d) Make the side KL (between ∠K = 40° and ∠L = 65°) 7 cm; then ASA gives T3 ≅ T1.
s: Part (a): 75°
Part (b): third angle 65°, ASA/AAS, ΔABC ≅ ΔDEF
Part (c): not congruent because the 7 cm side is in a different position
Part (d): sets KL = 7 cm, giving ASA

questions.a: (a) ∠OAB = ∠ODC and ∠OBA = ∠OCD (alternate angles). (b) ΔAOB ≅ ΔDOC by ASA. (c) AO = DO and BO = CO. (d) Yes, since AO = DO and BO = CO.

questions.q:
For a shed, roof frame 1 has ∠A = 50°, ∠B = 60° and AB = 3 m. Frame 2 has ∠P = 50°, ∠Q = 60° and PQ = 3 m. Frame 3 has ∠X = 50°, ∠Y = 60° and YZ = 3 m. Two sheds need 8 frames congruent to frame 1 in all. The contractor has 6 frames like frames 1 or 2 and 5 like frame 3. Option A: make 2 new frames at ₹2,500 each. Option B: hire 2 frames like frame 1 from a neighbouring school at ₹1,200 each, to be returned after 3 weeks. The sheds must stand for a year.
(a) Find the third angle of frame 1. (b) Are frames 1 and 2 congruent? Name the condition. (c) Are frames 1 and 3 congruent? Explain using where the 3 m side lies. (d) Which option should the contractor take? Decide.
questions.a: (a) 70°. (b) Yes, ASA: AB lies between ∠A and ∠B, and PQ between ∠P and ∠Q. (c) No: in frame 3 the 3 m side YZ lies opposite ∠X, not between the 50° and 60° angles, so it does not correspond to AB. (d) Making 2 new frames costs 2 x 2,500 = ₹5,000 and hiring 2 costs 2 x 1,200 = ₹2,400. Hiring is cheaper, but the hired frames go back after 3 weeks while the sheds must stand for a year, so make the new frames.
s: Part (a): 70°
Part (b): ASA from the positions of AB and PQ
Part (c): not congruent, as the 3 m side is in a different position
Part (d): ₹5,000 against ₹2,400 and a choice using the year-long need

questions.q:
Surveyor Reena checks whether two triangular plots are congruent. Plot 1 has ∠A = 48°, ∠C = 62° and BC = 40 m. For Plot 2 she measures ∠P = 48°, ∠Q = 70°, ∠R = 62° and QR = 40 m. Measuring an angle costs ₹600 and measuring a side costs ₹400. For Plot 3 she must choose between measuring two angles and one side, or all three sides. A pond blocks side CA, and a boat to measure it costs ₹700 extra.
(a) Find ∠B of Plot 1. (b) Are the two plots congruent? Name the condition. (c) What did Reena's four measurements of Plot 2 cost, and how much could she have saved? (d) Which plan should she use for Plot 3? Decide.
questions.a: (a) ∠B = 180° - 110° = 70°. (b) Yes, AAS: ∠A = ∠P, ∠B = ∠Q and BC = QR (the side opposite ∠A and ∠P). (c) 3 x 600 + 400 = ₹2,200; two angles and the side were enough (₹1,600), so she could have saved ₹600. (d) Two angles and a side cost ₹1,600; three sides cost 3 x 400 + 700 = ₹1,900. Use two angles and a side.
s: Part (a): 70°
Part (b): congruent by AAS
Part (c): ₹2,200 and a saving of ₹600
Part (d): ₹1,600 against ₹1,900, so angles-and-side

How many triangles can be drawn, and why? (c) Which special case of two sides and an angle does work, and why?

Part (b): two triangles and the reason
Part (c): RHS and the reason

(a) In tent A's triangle, which side is the hypotenuse? (b) Is tent B's triangle congruent to A's, and how far is B's stake from its pole? (c) What do the ropes of tents A and B together cost? (d) Should the third tent be built like A or like C? Decide.
questions.a: (a) The rope. (b) Yes, RHS (right angle, rope 5 m, pole 3 m), so B's stake is also 4 m from its pole. (c) 2 x 4 x 5 x 40 = ₹1,600. (d) Like A: ropes cost 4 x 5 x 40 = ₹800 against 4 x 5.5 x 40 = ₹880, and by RHS its stake is already known to be 4 m; choose C only if the extra shade is worth ₹80 and a site measurement.
s: Part (a): the rope
Part (b): RHS and 4 m
Part (d): compares ₹800 with ₹880 and the stake measurement, and decides

The supplier also offers eight more with sides of 12 cm and 15 cm, whose angles have never been measured, at ₹110 each with no returns. Measuring the angle of a board costs ₹20.
(a) Which of the twelve are congruent to P, and by which condition? (b) Why can the eight not yet be called congruent to P? (c) What is the payment for the twelve? (d) Should the shop take the eight unseen, or have each measured first? Decide.

(c) 12 x 150 = ₹1,800. (d) Measure first: 8 x 20 = ₹160, small against 8 x 110 = ₹880 that would be wasted with no returns if the boards turn out not to match.
s: Part (a): the twelve by RHS
Part (b): angles unknown, only two sides known
Part (d): measures first, comparing ₹160 with ₹880

questions.q: Explain in two steps why every angle of an equilateral triangle is 60°.
questions.a: The sides are equal, so the angles opposite them are equal. The three equal angles add up to 180°, so each is 180° / 3 = 60°.

180° divided by 3 gives 60°

questions.q: Show that a triangle with AB = AC cannot have ∠B = 90°.
questions.a: Since AB = AC, ∠B = ∠C. If ∠B = 90° then ∠C = 90°, and ∠B + ∠C = 180° already, leaving nothing for ∠A. The angles of a triangle must add up to 180° with ∠A greater than 0, so it cannot exist.

Concludes no angle is left for ∠A

Part (b): AB = BC gives ∠A = ∠C

questions.q:
An engineer compares three roof trusses, each an isosceles triangle with two equal rafters. The apex angle (between the rafters) is 50° for truss 1, 90° for truss 2 and 20° for truss 3. To keep the sideways push on the walls low, each base angle must be at least 60°. The trusses cost ₹40,000, ₹30,000 and ₹55,000, and the budget is ₹45,000.
(a) Find the base angle of each truss. (b) Which trusses meet the 60° rule? (c) What is the largest apex angle that still meets the rule, and what kind of triangle has it? (d) Which truss should be chosen? Decide using the rule, the costs and the budget.
questions.a: (a) 65°, 45° and 80°. (b) Trusses 1 and 3. (c) Base angle at least 60° means (180° - apex)/2 is at least 60°, so the apex is at most 60°; at exactly 60° all three angles are 60°, an equilateral triangle. (d) Truss 1 meets the rule at ₹40,000, within the budget; truss 3 is ₹10,000 over it; choose truss 1.
s: Part (b): trusses 1 and 3
Part (c): apex at most 60°, equilateral at the limit
Part (d): truss 1, citing rule, cost and budget

questions.q:
A rangoli group makes flower patterns from paper equilateral triangles of side 15 cm. Each flower uses triangles that meet at one centre point and fill the full turn of 360°. They need 18 flowers. Readymade triangles cost ₹4 each. One sheet costing ₹25 can be cut into 8 such triangles by the students.
(a) What is the angle of each triangle at the centre? (b) How many triangles meet at the centre of one flower? (c) How many triangles are needed in all, and what do readymade ones cost? (d) What do sheets cost, and which way should the group choose? Decide.
questions.a: (a) 60°. (b) 360° / 60° = 6. (c) 18 x 6 = 108 triangles; 108 x 4 = ₹432. (d) 108/8 = 13.5, so 14 sheets cost 14 x 25 = ₹350, which is ₹82 less; cutting sheets is cheaper, though readymade pieces save time and give neater triangles. Either choice is fine if the reason uses these costs.
s: Part (a): 60°
Part (b): 6 triangles
Part (c): 108 triangles and ₹432
Part (d): 14 sheets, ₹350, and a reasoned choice

Part (b): equal angles on a line, each 90°
Part (c): 32° and 58°

questions.q:
A tile shop cuts square tiles ABCD along the diagonal AC into two triangular ledges. Each square tile costs ₹30. Readymade triangular ledges cost ₹18 each. A hostel needs 48 triangular ledges.
(a) List the equal parts of ΔABC and ΔADC. (b) Write the congruence in two different ways. (c) In ΔABC, AB = BC and ∠B = 90°. Find ∠BAC. (d) Which option is cheaper for 48 ledges, and should the hostel take it? Decide using your earlier answers.
questions.a: (a) AB = AD, BC = DC and AC common. (b) ΔABC ≅ ΔADC and ΔABC ≅ ΔCDA. (c) The base angles are equal: (180° - 90°)/2 = 45°. (d) Cutting 24 tiles costs 24 x 30 = ₹720; readymade ledges cost 48 x 18 = ₹864. Cutting is ₹144 cheaper, and every pair is congruent by SSS.
s: Part (a): AB = AD, BC = DC, AC common
Part (b): two valid congruences
Part (c): 45°
Part (d): ₹720 versus ₹864 and a decision

questions.q:
Meera wants the width of a river without crossing it. A tree P stands on the far bank. She stands at Q on her bank so that PQ is at right angles to the bank. She walks along the bank 40 m to R, then 40 m further to S, turns at right angles away from the river and walks until the flag at R and the tree P are in line, at point T. She finds ST = 65 m. A bridge would cost ₹35,000 per metre of width and the town has ₹20 lakh.
(a) Name the three equal parts of ΔPQR and ΔTSR. (b) Write the congruence and name the condition. (c) What is PQ? (d) Can the town afford the bridge here? Decide.
questions.a: (a) QR = SR = 40 m, ∠Q = ∠S = 90°, ∠PRQ = ∠TRS (vertically opposite). (b) ΔPQR ≅ ΔTSR by ASA. (c) PQ = TS = 65 m. (d) Cost = 65 x 35,000 = ₹22,75,000, which is ₹2,75,000 more than ₹20 lakh, so not at this site.
s: Part (a): the three equal parts
Part (b): ASA
Part (c): 65 m
